text.headline: Knoxville Coffee Crawl: From Roasting Town to Third Places
text.text:
Research question: How did Knoxville’s coffee culture grow from an industrial roasting town into a city of independent coffee shops, and why have those shops become important gathering places in Knoxville today?

The tour starts with two historic stops in the Old City, then visits five present-day shops from the UT campus to South Knoxville.

Ratings are from Google Maps as of November 2026. Read a text-only version of this tour.

text.headline: History: JFG Coffee
text.text:
Historic stop · 1926–2000s

Address: 200 W. Jackson Ave. (now JFG Flats)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • JFG was named for founder James Franklin Goodson’s initials; its slogan was “The Best Part of the Meal.”
  • Roasting moved to Jackson Ave. in 1926; in the mid-1930s JFG moved into a former hat factory nearby, which is now the JFG Flats apartments.
  • Neely: “For 80 years, the northern part of downtown Knoxville smelled like roasting coffee.”
  • Reily Foods bought JFG in 1965; the restored JFG sign near the Gay Street Bridge is still a landmark.
  • Before JFG: coffee was sold downtown by the 1790s, and the Franklin Hotel at Gay and Main had a “coffee house” in the 1840s.
  • Idea: coffee here was an industry (jobs, smell, factories), not yet a social space.

Sources: Neely, “A Caffeinated History of Coffee & Tea in Knoxville” (Visit Knoxville, 2025); Know Your Knox: the JFG sign

text.headline: History: Old City Java
text.text:
Historic stop · opened 1990

Address: 109 S. Central St.

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • Opened in 1990, “several years before Starbucks got here,” and “struck some people as a strange fad” (Neely).
  • Possibly the oldest business still operating in the Old City.
  • In the 1960s most Knoxvillians drank instant coffee or Sanka; Old City Java marks the shift to the coffeehouse as a place to gather.
  • Idea: the start of the “third place” era in Knoxville.

Sources: Neely, “A Caffeinated History of Coffee & Tea in Knoxville” (Visit Knoxville, 2025)

text.headline: Capybara Coffee
text.text:
Tucked into University Commons, Capybara Coffee is about a five-minute walk from campus. Sadly, there are no real capybaras, but the vibes are adorable and the coffee is excellent.

Address: 2457 University Commons Way
Rating: 4.8/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • Centers Brazilian coffee culture and sources from Casa Brasil; also serves Smith Teamaker teas.
  • Partnered with UT’s Plant Sciences Club on a student plant-adoption event.
  • Idea: why is it popular with students? Location, community events, a distinct identity.

Sources: Visit Knoxville: Knoxville’s Coffee Scene; UT calendar: Plant Adoption with Capybara Coffee

text.headline: New Here Coffee
text.text:
Right beneath The Hub apartments on the Strip, New Here is just a street away from campus and one of the best study spots in town.

Address: 1915 Cumberland Ave.
Rating: 4.2/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • I found no news coverage of its opening or ownership. Ask the staff, or check its website or social media.
  • Idea: it sits under student housing on the Strip. How has Cumberland Ave’s redevelopment shaped where students gather?

Sources:

text.headline: Coffee 360
text.text:
In the heart of Fort Sanders, Coffee 360 serves a wide variety of flavors and baked goods, a convenient stop for students who live off campus. It also partners with local apartment complexes on monthly “Bagel Socials.”

Rating: 4.7/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • Check: I could not find this shop under the name “Coffee 360.” Confirm the name, address, and pin location. (The Coffee Underground is at 713 S. 17th St. in Fort Sanders.)
  • Idea: the “Bagel Socials” with apartment complexes are evidence of coffee shops building neighborhood community.

Sources:

text.headline: Jacks
text.text:
On Gay Street at the edge of the Old City, Jacks has a vibe unlike any other coffee shop in the area. Along with coffee, it sells plants and other fun goods, and it has a second location on North Central Street.

Address: 133 S. Gay St.
Rating: 4.4/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • Opened Feb. 2019 at 133 S. Gay St. by Katherine and Logan Higgins as a shop for local makers, with 17 Knoxville vendors at first.
  • Coffee and plants came later through partners Mark and Kendell Lily. A second location (“Jacks 2.0”) opened at 854 N. Central St. in 2021.
  • Check: one listing shows the Gay St. shop as closed. Confirm before presenting.
  • Idea: coffee shops as platforms for the local economy and local identity.

Sources: Inside of Knoxville: Jacks Opens Today (2019); Inside of Knoxville: Jacks’ Second Location (2021)

text.headline: Honeybee Coffee Co.
text.text:
Take a short trip across the river into South Knoxville and you’ll find Honeybee Coffee Co., one of the best coffee shops outside of downtown. On top of great coffee, it has views of the river and a large lounge to enjoy your latte in. Hours have changed recently, so check before you go.

Address: 700 Sevier Ave.
Rating: 4.5/5 on Google Maps (Nov. 2026)

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • Started as an Airstream coffee trailer downtown in 2014; opened its first shop here in January 2017.
  • The McMurry Building dates to about 1924; from 1939 it housed Charlie’s Cafe, which served workers from the nearby meatpacking plant and bus shop.
  • The shop is part of Sevier Avenue’s slow revival after decades of neglect.
  • In 2024 a failed ownership sale and a staff walkout closed most locations; as of July 2024 only this shop stayed open, with limited hours. Check: confirm its current status.
  • Idea: reuse of an old working-class building, and the fragility of local coffee businesses.

Sources: Knox Mercury: The Slow Rebirth of Sevier Avenue (2017); Knox News: Honeybee’s 10-year history (2024)

text.headline: Conclusion: Why These Shops Matter
text.text:
Your answer to the research question goes here.

Draft research notes (rewrite in your own words, then delete this box)

  • From factory to gathering place: coffee in Knoxville went from an industrial product (JFG) to a social experience (Old City Java onward).
  • Third places: each shop gives a specific community somewhere to be, whether students, local makers, or a reviving neighborhood.
  • Local identity: the shops sell Knoxville itself through local goods, historic buildings, and neighborhood events.
  • Limits: popularity is not permanence (Honeybee). Who might feel unwelcome or priced out?

text.text:
